case_data.title: Initiative for the Development of Artificial Intelligence
case_data.provide-a-brief-description-of-the-proje:
The Initiative for the Development of Artificial Intelligence (IDIA) led by Niyel, with its two phases, is a research and advocacy project that translates evidence into inclusive AI public policies across Francophone Africa,  from knowledge production to meaningful public participation. 
Over the first three years ( 2021-2024), the project laid the foundations for a policy research ecosystem on AI in Francophone Africa. In partnership with UNCHK, CURI, and IPAR, the project produced analyses covering Benin, Burkina Faso, Côte d'Ivoire, and Senegal, and translated them into direct engagement with decision-makers at national and regional levels. The research teams were able to identify the political, legal, institutional and ethical frameworks related to AI, draw up recommendations for the development of national documents on AI ethics in West Africa, present a data skills continuum, outline the state of AI development in the region, highlight the impact of AI on economic growth, the labor market and well-being of Africans, and document the state of AI resources in Senegal, with a focus on skills, resources and mastery of the regulatory framework. From the research conducted, findings capable of facilitating rapid and evidence-based decision-making by policymakers were produced for the second phase of the project. 
The goal is to convert the conversations initiated into concrete, measurable actions and to ensure that no community is left behind as AI governance frameworks take shape. During the second phase, the project : 
Created a structured space for dialogue on the role of AI in shaping the future of Francophone Africa, with accountability mechanisms for national and regional leaders -A technical workshop was conducted with representatives from five African francophone governments, ministries, research institutions such as the  Prosperous, Agricole, and Rural Initiative  (IPAR), The Centre of interdisciplinary excellency on AI for development ( CITADEL),  and regional bodies such as the African Union Development Agency (AUDA-NEPAD). One of the key outputs of the workshop is the development of the first francophone Guidelines for Ethical, Responsible, and Inclusive AI for Francophone Africa. The guidelines represent the result of a participatory approach, including technicians, policy makers, and experts, to provide a common normative foundation for countries in the region, grounded in shared principles and recognized international and African standards, to strengthen institutional capacities in AI governance, through practical recommendations tailored to countries specificity - to encourage the integration of ethics throughout the public policy lifecycle, from the design to the regulation of AI systems. 
Launched the NIYEL Fellowship - a nine-month capacity-building program designed to equip public sector professionals with the skills, tools, and network needed to influence policies and practices within their institutions and their sector. Through targeted training, mentorship, and collaborative learning, the program strengthens participants’ advocacy, leadership, and communication skills, enabling them to champion ethical and responsible decision-making in Artificial Intelligence. The Fellowship also contributes to the development of more inclusive, ethical, and context-responsive AI policies and governance frameworks. By fostering peer learning, strengthening regional networks, and facilitating strategic partnerships among policymakers, AI experts, and other key stakeholders, the program helps build a vibrant community of leaders committed to advancing responsible and inclusive AI across the region. 
The project created the space for civil society, academia, innovators, and grand public to interact and exchange ideas on AI development and its impact on our daily lives. These open spaces provide a safe space to address their concerns.   
Collaboration and partnership with civil society organizations: The project facilitates technical and funding support to 10 civil society organizations from the West Africa region, to conduct national mobilization on AI and to engage with communities in concrete actions to inform decision makers and influence existing and current policy processes on AI at national and regional levels. The civil society organizations from Benin, Mali, Togo, Burkina Faso, the Ivory Coast, Senegal, the RDC, Guinea, Niger, and Cameroon shared a common goal, which is to improve the human condition through knowledge translation and contribute to crafting policies that address societal challenges related to AI understanding, use, and adoption in their respective countries. They make sure communities, and underrepresented groups are in the room to discuss AI risks, impact, and opportunities.
case_data.project-title: Initiative for the Development of Artificial Intelligence
case_data.why-is-this-project-important-to-include:
As the global AI governance debate accelerates, IDIA offers a documented, multi-year example of how research translation, civil society engagement, and policy dialogue can work together to make AI governance genuinely participatory.  IDIA is important to be included in the case book because: 
 
IDIA built participation into its architecture from the start:  researchers, policymakers, and civil society co-constructed the research agenda and outputs rather than being consulted after the fact. 
Research on AI readiness in Benin, Burkina Faso, Côte d'Ivoire, and Senegal was translated into policy briefs, national strategy inputs, and parliamentary engagement,  closing the gap between knowledge and action. 
Unlike many global AI initiatives, IDIA is led by African institutions. It models what it means for the Global South to set its own AI governance agenda rather than adapt frameworks designed elsewhere. 
The IDIA methodology, throughout the two phases:  research consortia, policy translation, civil society mobilization, and policy engagement, offers a learning model for participatory AI governance that other Francophone and African countries can adapt. 
IDIA provides concrete evidence of what this looks like in practice across Francophone Africa, a region of 400 million people whose perspectives have been largely absent from global AI norm-setting processes.

AI Development: Shape the development of AI tools
Empowerment: Build community power with respect to AI
